newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia struggling with pollution blight.
newsitem.headline: Russia struggling with pollution blight.

text.p: Russia is so polluted it would have to spend its entire national income for many years to clean up the ecological hazards threatening its citizens' health, the government's top environmental official said on Friday.
He said many of Russia's problems were inherited from the Soviet past, when smoking chimney stacks were a symbol of progress. But outdated factories continued to pose a risk.

"We consider about half the territory of the Russian Federation to be ecologically unacceptable, where pollution threatens health," Viktor Danilov-Danilyan, head of the state committee for the environment, told Reuters in an interview.
"A complete clean up of the environment would cost many times more than the annual gross domestic product," he said.
Russia's GDP in 1996 was about $400 billion.
"The problem of radioactive waste, at a minimum, would cost $700 billion," he said. "To clean up the drinking water supply would cost about $200 billion."

The problem is especially acute in Moscow because of pollution from cars, in the Ural mountains, a centre of metallurgy and heavy industry, as well as areas of the north and Far East where outdated factories are pumping out pollution.
Danilov-Danilyan said nuclear waste around the Mayak reactor in Chelyabinsk posed a danger as large amounts of radioactive waste are stored there.
"As far as potential threats to the economy and people's health the situation with nuclear waste is very threatening as it is not kept in proper conditions," he said.

As an example of the threat he cited a once-secret 1957 accident in which tons of radioactive waste stored near Chelyabinsk spread across much of the Urals region after an explosion in a nuclear waste storage site.
Another vexing environmental problem facing Russia is the destruction of 40,000 tons of chemical weapons pledged by Moscow under international agreements.

"This is an extraordinarily complex problem because first of all the storage facilities for chemical weapons are incredibly worn out and corroded," he said. "To continue to store them as they are today in many cases would be incredibly dangerous."
On a daily basis, the most serious problem facing Russians is the surface water supply, which Danilov-Danilyan called unsatisfactory for 60 percent of the population.
Many Russians boil their drinking water as a precaution, and the more affluent in recent years have begun installing filters in their kitchens.
Despite the catalogue of dangers facing the population, Russia will be unable to address many of its environmental problems until the economy improves, Danilov-Danilyan said.
"The amount of pollution dumped during communism was so great that to free ourselves from it, we need a much longer amount of time and more measures than have been adopted," he told Reuters.
"Only then can the ecological situation improve," he continued. "Up until now it has not improved in practically the entire country, and it has even worsened in the most polluted industrial areas."
In 1997 Russian officials will work out a long-term plan sought by President Boris Yeltsin to improve the environment, but it is likely to take many years before decisive action is taken, he said.
